newsitem.title: POLAND: AUSTRIA'S SCHUESSEL BACKS POLAND'S NATO GOALS.
newsitem.headline: AUSTRIA'S SCHUESSEL BACKS POLAND'S NATO GOALS.

text.p: Austria's Foreign Minister Wolfgang Schuessel declared strong support in Warsaw on Wednesday for Poland's bid to join the European Union and NATO, saying Central Europe should not be a buffer zone.

"We strongly support Poland's entry to European security structures and its membership in the EU," Schuessel, who is also Austria's vice-chancellor, said after talks with Polish Foreign Minister Dariusz Rosati.

"I have always thought the idea of creating -- between the EU and the countries of the former Soviet Union -- a form of buffer zone made up of the countries of Central and Eastern Europe, is irrational and irrelevant," he told reporters.
He said it would promote the stability of Poland, Russia and the European union itself if countries of Central and Eastern Europe took part in NATO and EU structures.
It would also be good for Austria, which had strong economic ties and investments in the region.
Austria itself is not in NATO and has been neutral for more than four decades.
But Poland is seeking all the support it can get for its full membership of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation, which is strongly opposed by Moscow as a threat to Russian security.
Rosati told reporters that Austria had been very friendly and helpful to Poland over the last decade.
Warsaw, which escaped Soviet domination in 1989, expects to be among the first countries to be invited to start NATO entry talks at the pact's Madrid summit in July, and to join in 1999.
But it is anxious that pressure from Russia and Western opponents could cause delays or some watered down, second-class NATO membership, weakened by concessions to Moscow.

Rosati is to hold talks in Washington on Thursday, at Poland's request, with U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, ahead of the March 19 Helsinki summit between the U.S. and Russian Presidents Bill Clinton and Boris Yeltsin.

Schuessel arrived late in Warsaw for the first official visit by an Austrian foreign minister in six years, because fog delayed his flight. He was later due to meet Poland's president Aleksander Kwasniewski.
